# Summary: Jacek Karpiński
Jacek Karpiński (1927–2010) was a pioneering Polish computer engineer born into a family of intellectuals and mountaineers. Despite losing sight temporarily and being seriously injured in World War II during his involvement in Polish resistance efforts, he resumed education and graduated from Warsaw University of Technology in 1951. He developed several innovative computing devices, including the AAH (Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics), AKAT-1 (the world’s first transistor-based differential equations analyzer), and KAR-65 (a high-speed Polish computer). Most notably, Karpiński led the design of the K-202 minicomputer in the early 1970s, which featured advanced architecture and was competitive with Western machines. However, despite its technical excellence, the K-202 suffered from political and industrial opposition that prevented its mass production.
Karpiński spent time on a UNESCO scholarship in the United States, where he met leading computer scientists but chose to return to Poland. He also developed early artificial neural network devices like the Polish perceptron and worked on data processing machines. Facing censorship and political struggles in communist Poland, Karpiński left technological development in 1978, later moved to Switzerland, and eventually returned to Poland. Posthumously, he was honored with the Commander's Cross of Polonia Restituta. Controversy surrounds his cooperation with Polish intelligence services during the Cold War, although historians suggest this was motivated by naivete and limited to technological reporting. Karpiński is recognized as a visionary whose innovative contributions were hindered by political factors in Poland.
